cards.title: How a motor spins
cards.summary: Magnets push and pull. Switch which coil is a magnet, and the rotor keeps chasing the next one.
cards.body: Run a current through a coil of wire and it becomes an electromagnet with a north and a south pole. Put permanent magnets on a part that can turn (the rotor), and it twists until opposite poles line up. A motor never lets that happen: just before they line up, it switches the current to the next coil. The rotor is always chasing a target that keeps moving ahead of it, so it spins. Faster switching means faster spinning; more current means a stronger pull (more torque).

cards.summary: The same four steps, thousands of times a second in a drone motor.

cards.title: The force on a wire
cards.summary: Double the current, double the push. That's why motors get hot when they work hard.

cards.title: Brushed vs brushless
cards.summary: Old motors switch coils with rubbing brushes. Brushless ones use a tiny computer instead.
cards.body: A brushed motor switches its coils mechanically: carbon brushes rub on a split ring (the commutator) on the shaft, so the current flips by itself as it turns. Simple and cheap, but the brushes spark, wear out and waste energy. A brushless motor flips it around: the coils sit still on the outside or inside, the magnets spin, and an electronic speed controller (ESC) switches the current. No rubbing parts, so it runs cooler, lasts longer and can spin much faster. Drones, electric cars and hard drives all use brushless motors.

cards.title: Inside a drone motor
cards.summary: This kind is an outrunner: the magnets are in the bell that spins around the coils.

cards.title: The ESC: the motor's conductor
cards.summary: A chip that flips the current between three wires, up to tens of thousands of times a second.
cards.body: A brushless motor has three wires. The ESC (electronic speed controller) connects two of them to the battery at a time, one positive and one negative, in a six-step pattern. Each step pulls the rotor a little further round. To know when to switch, it either reads Hall sensors that feel where the magnets are, or listens to the voltage the spinning magnets induce in the coil that's switched off. Speed is set by switching the power on and off very fast (PWM) to control the average voltage.

cards.title: Six-step switching, in code
cards.summary: Each line: which wire goes to + and which to −. Six steps make one electrical turn.

visual.text:
STEPS = [("A","B"), ("A","C"), ("B","C"),
         ("B","A"), ("C","A"), ("C","B")]

step = 0
while running:
    plus, minus = STEPS[step]
    connect(plus, minus)
    wait_for_next_magnet()
    step = (step + 1) % 6

cards.title: How does it know where the magnets are?
cards.summary: Tiny sensors that feel a magnetic field, or a clever trick: listening to the motor itself.

cards.title: Why do brushes spark?
cards.summary: Breaking a current in a coil fights back with a voltage spike.

cards.title: Every motor is secretly a generator
cards.summary: Spin it by hand and electricity comes out. Electric cars use this to brake.

cards.title: Motors are everywhere
cards.summary: Your phone's vibration, a fridge, a lift, a Mars rover: all motors.
cards.body: A phone vibrates with a tiny motor spinning an off-centre weight. Hard drives spin a platter at 7,200 turns a minute. A modern car has dozens of small motors for windows, seats, mirrors, wipers and pumps, before you even count an electric car's drive motor. Robots are mostly motors with sensors and a computer: every joint in a robot arm is a motor with a gearbox and a sensor that measures its angle.

cards.title: Where does the energy go?
cards.summary: How much of the energy becomes motion, roughly. The rest turns into heat.
